'''''Eucalyptus viminalis''''', commonly known as the '''manna gum''', '''white gum''' or '''ribbon gum''',<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus viminalis'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_viminalis_subsp._viminalis.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=16 January 2020}}</ref> is a species of small to very tall tree that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to south-eastern Australia. It has smooth bark, sometimes with rough bark near the base, lance-shaped to curved adult leaves, flower buds in groups of three or seven, white flowers and cup-shaped or hemispherical fruit.

==Description==
''Eucalyptus viminalis'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|50|m}}, sometimes to {{cvt|90|m}}, and forms a [[lignotuber]]. It has smooth, often powdery, white to pale brown bark that is shed in long ribbons, sometimes hanging on the upper branches, and sometimes with rough, fibrous bark on the lower trunk. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]], lance-shaped to curved or oblong leaves {{cvt|25-150|mm}} long, {{cvt|5-35|mm}} wide and arranged in opposite pairs. Adult leaves are arranged alternately, the same shade of green on both sides, lance-shaped to curved, {{cvt|85-232|mm}} long and {{cvt|8-30|mm}} wide, tapering to a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|10-25|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in groups of three or seven on an unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|4-10|mm}} long, the individual buds sessile or on [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] up to {{cvt|5|mm}} long. Mature buds are oval to spindle-shaped, {{cvt|5-9|mm}} long and {{cvt|3-6|mm}} wide with a conical, rounded or beaked [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering occurs from December to May and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody, cup-shaped or hemispherical [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|3-8|mm}} long and {{cvt|5-9|mm}} wide with the valves prominently protruding.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=Ken |title=''Eucalyptus viminalis'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Eucalyptus~viminalis |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=16 January 2020}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus viminalis'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20viminalis |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=16 January 2020}}</ref><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Brooker |first1=M. Ian H. |last2=Slee |first2=Andrew V. |title=''Eucalyptus viminalis'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/4986f096-0923-4a4b-8d65-fbb209ae0042 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=16 January 2020}}</ref><ref name="costermans">{{cite book |last1=Costermans |first1=Leon F. |title=Trees of Victoria and adjoining areas |date=2006 |publisher=Costermans Publishing |location=Frankston, Victoria |isbn=0-9599105-4-9 |page=76}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus viminalis'' was first formally described in 1806 by [[Jacques Labillardière]] in his book ''[[Novae Hollandiae Plantarum Specimen]]''.<ref name="Labill.">{{cite book |last1=Labillardière |first1=Jacques |title=Novae Hollandiae Plantarum Specimen (volume 2) |date=1806 |volume=2 |publisher=Ex typographia Dominæ Huzard,1804-1806 |location=Paris |pages=12–13 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/40882044#page/12/mode/1up |access-date=16 January 2020}}</ref><ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus viminalis''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/454897 |publisher=APNI|access-date=16 January 2020}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''viminalis'') is a [[Latin]] word meaning "bearing shoots or ribbons for [[wicker]] work.<ref name="CANBR" />

It is also usually smooth-barked and has flower buds mostly in groups of three.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="RBGS" />

According to the early Australian ethnographer [[Alfred William Howitt]], the name ''wurundjeri'', in his transcription ''urunjeri'', refers to ''E. viminalis'' which is common along [[Yarra River|Birrarung]].<ref name="book">{{cite book |last1=Ellender |first1=Isabel |last2=Christiansen |first2=Peter |title=People of the Merri Merri: the Wurundjeri in colonial days |date=2001 |publisher=Merri Creek Management Committee |location=East Brunswick, Vic. |isbn=0-9577728-0-7 |page=35}}</ref>{{rp|109}} Some modern reports of [[Wurundjeri]] traditional lore state that their [[ethnonym]] combines a word, ''wurun'', meaning ''manna gum'' and ''djeri'', a species of grub found in the tree, and take the word therefore to mean "[[Witchetty grub|Witchetty Grub]] People".<ref name="book" />{{rp|35}}

Some common names included white gum or swamp gum of Tasmania, manna gum, grey gum, blue gum, and drooping gum.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |author=J. H. Maiden |url=https://primo-slnsw.hosted.exlibrisgroup.com/primo-explore/fulldisplay?docid=SLNSW_ALMA21105097830002626&context=L&vid=SLNSW&search_scope=EEA&tab=default_tab&lang=en_US |title=The useful native plants of Australia: Including Tasmania |publisher=Turner and Henderson, Sydney |year=1889}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Subspecies ''cygnetensis'', commonly known as the rough-barked manna gum, grows in the higher rainfall areas of South Australia, including [[Kangaroo Island]] and the southern [[Mount Lofty Ranges]] and as far east as the [[Grampians National Park|Grampians]] in Victoria.<ref name="Nicolle" /><ref name="RBGV1" /><ref name="CANBR1">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus viminalis'' subsp. ''cygnetensis'' |url=http://keyserver.lucidcentral.org:8080/euclid/data/02050e02-0108-490e-8900-0e0601070d00/media/Html/Eucalyptus_viminalis_subsp._cygnetensis.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=16 January 2020}}</ref> Subspecies ''hentyensis'', commonly known as the western Tasmanian sand gum, grows in sandy soil on the west coast of Tasmania, north from [[Strahan, Tasmania|Strahan]].<ref name="JABG2" /><ref name="CANBR2">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus viminalis'' subsp. ''hentyensis'' |url=http://keyserver.lucidcentral.org:8080/euclid/data/02050e02-0108-490e-8900-0e0601070d00/media/Html/Eucalyptus_viminalis_subsp._hentyensis.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=16 January 2020}}</ref> Subspecies ''pryoriana'', commonly known as the Gippsland manna gum, grows in sandy, coastal soil from the [[Bellarine Peninsula]] to Lake Tyers in the [[Gippsland Lakes]] in Victoria.<ref name="Muelleria" /><ref name="RBGV2" /><ref name="CANBR3">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus viminalis'' subsp. ''pryoriana'' |url=http://keyserver.lucidcentral.org:8080/euclid/data/02050e02-0108-490e-8900-0e0601070d00/media/Html/Eucalyptus_viminalis_subsp._pryoriana.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=16 January 2020}}</ref> Subspecies ''siliceana'' is known only from the Wail State Forest in the [[Wimmera]] region of Victoria, where it grows in deep sand.<ref name="Rule" /><ref name="RBGV3" /> Subspecies ''viminalis'' is widely distributed and abundant in the well-watered areas of south-eastern Australia, from the coast and ranges of New South Wales, the southern half of Victoria, the [[Eyre Peninsula]] and Kangaroo Island in south-eastern South Australia. It also occurs in Tasmania where some specimens are almost {{cvt|90|m}} tall.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="RBGS" />

==Uses==
[[Indigenous Australian]]s used the wood of the tree to make shields and wooden bowls.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/gardens/education/programs/pdfs/aboriginal_plant_use_and_technology.pdf|title=Aboriginal Plant use and Technology |access-date=11 November 2016|publisher=Australian National Botanic Garden}}</ref>

The tree produces a sweet, white, crumbly [[manna]] from its bark. Valued by [[Aboriginal Australians|Aboriginal]] people, this sugary substance forms when sap exudes and dries in the hot summer air, eventually falling to the ground in small irregular lumps. There is debate over the cause of the sap leakage, with some attributing it to [[cicada]] borings and others to the activity of a [[gall]]-making insect.<ref name=":0" />
